records.title: Climate of Change at OMSI
records.dek: Portland's science museum designed a climate exhibition around how visitors feel, not just what they learn, letting them choose their route by mood and readiness.
summary: The Oregon Museum of Science and Industry built its bilingual Climate of Change exhibition to address the anxiety and hopelessness people bring to the subject, structuring it as an emotional arc from heart to head to hope to hand.

Instead of a fixed route, the floor plan, shaped with advice from local Native American youth, opens onto four directions so visitors can pick a theatre of community stories, an immersive space, an art gallery or hands-on science according to whether they feel anxious, energised, curious or reflective.

Signature moments include a LIDAR-driven projection room where the environment grows from visitors who stand still, a quiet sphere space for reflection, and community-authored content that turns participation into co-ownership.
records.why: For Education, it shows how a school's learning spaces and open days can be designed around a student's or parent's emotional state as much as the content. For Community and Retail, it offers a model for public spaces that let visitors choose a calm or energetic path on each visit.
records.excerpt: OMSI designed the exhibition for the emotional experience of meeting climate change, on the view that feeling shapes a person's willingness to engage.

keyInsights: Designing for the emotion a visitor arrives with can matter as much as the information you want them to leave with.
Non-linear layouts that offer clear, named choices give people agency and let each visitor self-select the experience they are ready for.
Moving communities from consultation to co-ownership of content builds trust and lets people see themselves in a place.
Responsive technology can reward slowing down rather than activity, creating moments of presence and connection between strangers.

Each route suits a different emotional state, so people meet a difficult subject on their own terms and can rest, reflect or experiment as they need.

why.body: Letting visitors choose what they are ready to encounter keeps an anxiety-inducing topic approachable rather than overwhelming.

transfer.how: Design mall zones as clearly signposted choices, such as calm, social or active, so visitors can shape a visit to their mood on arrival.

Offer resort guests a responsive quiet space where light and sound react to stillness, giving a restorative pause between activities.

records.title: BLOOM Joondalup: a Luna Light journey through a public park
records.dek: A Western Australian civic park became a self-paced night-time story told through the eyes of a native bee, drawing most visitors from beyond the local area.
summary: BLOOM Joondalup turned an existing public park into a chaptered night walk that followed a native blue-banded bee, using the park's trees, paths and open spaces as part of the narrative rather than as a backdrop.

Laservision and the City of Joondalup layered lasers through the tree canopy, a 20-metre water screen, motion-responsive lighting and zone-specific soundscapes, alternating intimate botanical scenes with larger moments of spectacle so the route suited families and mixed ages.
The run was extended by a week in response to demand, sold more than 75,000 tickets, drew most visitors from outside the area and generated an estimated A$7.8 million in visitor spending.
records.why: For Community and Retail, it shows how existing parks, plazas and boulevards can become an after-dark destination with a narrative route, turning an ordinary evening visit into a reason to travel. It is equally relevant to resort grounds where guests look for something to do after dinner.
records.excerpt: The park was not just the venue; its canopy, paths and open spaces became the storytelling medium itself.

records.title: Chromatic pavilions and modular play structures activate historic Istanbul Rami Library
records.dek: Milimetrik Architects turned a heritage library into an eleven-day family festival, using open-ended play volumes and house-shaped book pavilions to draw around 825,000 visitors.
summary: For AileFest 2026, Istanbul's historic Rami Library became a 91,000-sqm family festival, with its courtyard and interior halls reworked into one connected landscape for play, learning and culture over eleven days.

Rather than fixed play equipment, the courtyard was filled with modular geometric volumes, abstract shelters and colourful gathering points scaled to different ages, leaving children free to invent their own use.

Indoors, the book fair dropped the usual grid of booths for pitched house-shaped pavilions, primary-coloured stands and graphic floors, all built in temporary timber and steel so the heritage fabric was left untouched.
records.why: For Community and Retail, this shows how a family event day in a plaza or mall atrium can feel like a destination by swapping standard booths and rides for open-ended, age-scaled play landscapes. Education can borrow the same thinking for open days, where the arrival courtyard sets the tone for parents and children.
records.excerpt: The designers chose semi-structured, child-scaled volumes over rigid play equipment, letting families circulate freely and invent their own ways to play.

records.title: Disney Adventure
records.dek: Disney Cruise Line reworked an unfinished mega-ship into a floating destination, organising it as a set of story-led districts around a central open-air garden.
summary: Disney Cruise Line acquired a partially built vessel and spent more than three years reimagining it as its largest ship, designed as a destination rather than simply a means of transport.

The ship is arranged as a collection of named themed areas, from Marvel Landing to San Fransokyo Street, anchored by Disney Imagination Garden, an open-air gathering space with a castle and a Garden Stage fitted with 3-deck-high LED screens.

Across these areas guests find aquatic play, outdoor entertainment, themed dining and interactive attractions, while separate brand collaborations and stores, signature shows and open-air performances add further layers to the visit.
records.why: For Retail and Community, it shows how a large site can be read as a sequence of distinct story districts around one central gathering space, shaping how a family moves through a mall visit or a weekend in the neighbourhood. For Hospitality, it points to resort stays where each zone offers its own play, dining and performance.
records.excerpt: The themed areas are designed to be used, not just admired: places to play, eat, watch shows and explore, rather than scenic backdrops.

records.title: Cosm's Shared Reality cinematic experiences
records.dek: Cosm wraps classic films in 12K LED domes, themed venues and scene-timed menus, giving fans a reason to watch familiar titles together rather than at home.
summary: Cosm plays well-known films unchanged at the centre of 87-foot LED domes, while custom screen extensions carry each film's world around and above the audience as the story moves.
The experience reaches beyond the screen through lighting, sensory touches, interactive installations, and tasting and cocktail menus drawn from each film, served to the seat and timed to scenes.

Nearly all initial showings of the first title sold out within two weeks and the run was extended twice, and Universal has since joined Warner Bros. as a second studio partner, with a slate spanning sci-fi, family, horror and animation.
records.why: For Retail, it shows how a mall entertainment visit can become a destination worth leaving the sofa for, by building a shared, multi-sensory event around content people already love. For Hospitality, scene-timed themed menus point to F&B that is choreographed with the moment rather than simply served alongside it.
records.excerpt: Cosm leaves the original film untouched and instead enlarges the room around it, so the emotional pull of a familiar story grows when it is shared with a crowd.

records.title: Gravity Haus wants to make mountain life a membership
records.dek: A US mountain hospitality brand bundles rooms, workspaces and gyms into tiered memberships, designing around the time-pressed parent who may not need a bed.
summary: Gravity Haus operates 13 properties across the western US and British Columbia that combine hotel rooms, workspaces and gyms. Its target guest is the busy parent or professional who wants more mountain days, not the hardcore enthusiast. Its signature use case is a family day trip, with higher membership tiers granting workspace, gym and gear-storage access without an overnight stay.

Memberships start with a $450 annual tier offering lodging discounts and rise through property, network and seasonal options. Subscription income lets the company keep the fees it charges hotel assets lower.
The model's success depends on renewals, repeat stays and on-property spending covering the discounts and the retrofit costs, and on explaining an unfamiliar bundled fee.
records.why: For Hospitality, it reframes the day visit: a family could use a resort as a base for work, fitness and meals while children attend activities, without booking a room. For Community, it suggests membership tiers that turn amenities into an everyday base for residents.
records.excerpt: The property shapes almost every part of the family's day, and the business earns from someone who does not always need a bed.

summary: Founded by a former educator turned innkeeper, Lark Hotels has grown to 63 properties across four brands, each built around the character of its building and destination rather than a uniform look.

records.title: Alaska Airlines Flagship Lounge by Graham Baba Architects
records.dek: At Seattle-Tacoma airport, Alaska Airlines moves away from the exclusive business lounge, using a staged entry and four distinct zones to offer every guest a refuge.
summary: Graham Baba Architects designed Alaska Airlines' flagship lounge at SeaTac as a warm, welcoming refuge from the concourse, deliberately moving away from the sleek, exclusive model of traditional airport lounges.

The space is divided into four lightly screened zones (an entry, a casual bistro, a quiet relaxation area and a bar), each with its own furniture, acoustics, materials and lighting so guests can choose the atmosphere that suits them.

A staged arrival sequence, from a wide concourse window and guiding oak frames to a fireplace view and a concierge desk, is combined with work by local fabricators and artists to root the experience in the Pacific Northwest.

records.title: Why Nespresso brought its loyalty programme back from dormancy
records.dek: Nespresso has revived its early-2000s club in the US, swapping points for personalised rewards, shared passions and access money cannot buy.
summary: Nespresso has relaunched its dormant Nespresso Club in North America, reframing loyalty around community and personalisation rather than a points ledger.

Rewards respond to how members engage, such as trying limited blends, joining barista classes, visiting boutiques or recycling capsules, and range from recipe demonstrations to an Ambassador tier and partner experiences like a Cannes red carpet invitation.
An EY loyalty leader adds that the strongest perks often remove friction and make customers feel known, while the core programme must stay worthwhile for every member, not just top spenders.
records.why: For Retail and Community, the model shows how a mall visit or a neighbourhood event can become a recognised act of belonging, with rewards tied to participation rather than spend alone.

records.title: Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
records.dek: A Copenhagen shop for rare and independent books uses modular, movable furniture and a dedicated red room to shift between bookstore, gallery, listening space and event venue.
summary: Simone Book Services in Copenhagen sells rare and independent books and magazines, but its interior is designed to flex into an exhibition gallery, listening room or venue for launches and informal gatherings.

Architect Derya Arpac led a deliberately un-Scandinavian scheme with commissioned pieces from several designers, including cherry-wood shelving, a zippered leather counter, modular aluminium magazine displays and mobile trolleys that invite visitors to move books around.

A small, David Lynch-inspired red room offers scope for intimate events and exhibitions, and the store has already hosted a book launch, a curated library for ASICS and a fashion pop-up, with changing artwork and future reading objects extending the offer.
records.why: For Retail, it shows how a single unit can be designed to change role across a mall visit, from shop to gallery to event space, giving repeat visitors a reason to return. For Community, it suggests how neighbourhood amenities could host launches and small gatherings within everyday spaces.
records.excerpt: The founders set out to make a place people visit to be inspired, not simply to buy, pairing a passion for books with a passion for design.

summary: Terreno Barrio Hotel in Palma pairs a restored 1935 apartment block, which holds reception, restaurant, bar, club and roof bar, with a new timber-and-cork building wrapped around a public plaza.

records.title: MVRDV designs Essen Central Library as public "living room" in Germany
records.dek: A six-storey former department store in Essen becomes a civic library designed around third-place thinking, welcoming visitors whether or not they come with a purpose.
summary: MVRDV, working with Meyer Architekten and third-place specialist Includi, has turned the Boeckerhaus department store on Kennedyplatz into an 11,000-square-metre central library conceived as a social and cultural hub rather than a book archive.

Drawing on Ray Oldenburg's third-place theory, the design aims to feel inclusive to everyone, with a glazed facade that puts reading, working and conversation on show to the street, a ground-floor cafe to draw in passersby and a rooftop events space.

Inside, red bookshelf clusters called media villages, lightening in tone floor by floor, define soft play, gaming pods, hobby zones, makerspaces and music rooms, supported by warm wood, plants, varied seating and blue wayfinding signage.
records.why: For Retail, it shows how an underused department-store volume can be reimagined as a reason to visit a mall even without a shopping errand, while for Community it offers a template for amenity spaces residents use as an everyday living room.
records.excerpt: "It becomes a living room that is open and inviting for all of Essen's diverse citizens" - Fokke Moerel, MVRDV

records.title: Light and shadow meet at One Bryant Park
records.dek: A new New York restaurant near Times Square uses Japanese ideas of filtered light and preserved shadow to turn three dining rooms into a calm retreat from the street.
summary: One Bryant Park on 42nd Street is a single restaurant offering three distinct dining experiences: a main dining room and bar, an omakase counter in Kumiko Room, and Kappo Sono, which is due to open in November.
Studio Canall designed each room with its own mood, tied together by the interplay of light and shadow and the meeting of Eastern and Western design.
Light is handled deliberately throughout, filtered through oak slats, backlit kumiko lattice and concealed fixtures, keeping darker pockets so that wood, plaster and metal textures can be felt.
records.why: For Hospitality and mall-based F&B in Retail, it shows how the moment a guest steps in from a busy street can be designed as a shift into calm, using lighting that keeps shadow rather than lighting a room evenly.
records.excerpt: The restaurant was conceived as a retreat from the Times Square bustle, meant to feel like standing in the shade of a forest.

records.dek: As hotels rush to call themselves longevity destinations, a roadmap argues that credibility comes from medical governance, residential-feeling design and a relationship that continues long after checkout.
summary: The article argues that longevity has become a marketing label that many luxury hotels use loosely, and that lasting value will go to properties that can clinically stand behind the word.

It sets out the choices owners face, from building their own clinic as Six Senses did in Ibiza to hosting partners such as Clinique La Prairie at One&Only One Za'abeel, HUM2N at Six Senses London and Mayrlife at Rosewood Vienna.

Its central experiential idea is that clinical credibility must be delivered without making the guest feel like a patient, through residential-style treatment rooms, data shared as conversation, and a care manager and membership that carry the relationship beyond departure.
records.why: For Hospitality, the after-checkout moment is where a wellness stay can become an ongoing relationship through follow-up and membership. For Development, the advice to plan a clinical area as a separable part of the building, with its own access and licensing path, is a useful principle at the master-planning stage.
records.excerpt: "The word longevity is easy to buy and hard to earn." - Nicolas Frangos

opps.title: Separable wellness wing
opps.text: Residents and visitors enter a wellness or clinical area through its own dedicated access, designed so the operator can change without disrupting the hotel or community around it.

keyInsights: Premium guests want medical credibility without feeling like patients, so clinical spaces should feel residential and results should be shared as a conversation.
The lasting value of a wellness programme lies in continuity, such as memberships and repeat measurements, rather than a single intensive week.
A single care manager who spans planning, the stay and follow-up mirrors the butler model and is something hospitality can supply better than a clinic alone.
Disciplined language matters: properties without clinical services can still add value through better sleep environments and trained staff without overclaiming.

records.title: The second booking: your regular came back through Booking.com, and your system thinks she's new
records.dek: Booking.com's email aliases and withheld phone numbers mean a hotel's returning guests can check in as strangers, with their preferences and history left behind.
summary: Booking.com's Genius programme rewards frequent travellers with hotel-funded discounts, so a guest's loyalty can attach to the app rather than to the property she already knows.

Because Booking.com forwards messages through a unique alias email for each reservation and no longer passes on phone numbers, hotel systems that match on these details often treat a returning guest as new, leaving her room preference, anniversary or allergy unseen.

The author argues that the hotel's real advantage is the guest's time on site, and urges properties to audit their repeat-guest data, collect real contact details at the desk and check every Booking.com arrival against past guests by name.
records.why: For Aldar's hotels, the arrival and check-in moment is where a returning guest either feels remembered or is treated as a stranger; recognition depends on matching guests by name and details captured on site, not on booking-channel data alone.
records.excerpt: The guests a booking platform retains most effectively can be the very ones a hotel is least able to recognise when they walk back in.
records.oppText: Every third-party arrival is checked against past stays by name before check-in, so a returning guest is greeted as a regular, finds her preferred room and remembered details in place, and receives her next-stay offer directly from the hotel.

opps.title: Welcome back, by name
opps.text: Every third-party arrival is checked against past stays by name before check-in, so a returning guest is greeted as a regular, finds her preferred room and remembered details in place, and receives her next-stay offer directly from the hotel.

keyInsights: Guest recognition fails quietly when systems match returning guests on email or phone alone, so matching on name and details collected at check-in matters.

Booking.com's alias emails and withheld phone numbers can strip a returning guest of her history, so preferences such as room choice, anniversaries and allergies need to live on a profile the hotel controls.
The stay itself, with no intermediary present, is the hotel's best opportunity to ask for a guest's real email and win her next booking directly.
Auditing how many repeat guests returned through Booking.com, and the commission paid on them, reveals what a property spends to host guests who already knew it.
records._benchWhyNot: Opinion piece on OTA distribution and data gaps rather than one brand's copyable customer-facing practice.

records.title: Jaguar designs Knightsbridge flagship to be a physical expression of the Type 01 electric car
records.dek: Jaguar has turned its London showroom into a destination led by a chef's restaurant, with interiors that echo its new car and private sales spaces below.
summary: Jaguar has rebuilt its Knightsbridge flagship as a destination rather than a conventional car showroom, and it is currently the only place where the public can see the new Type 01.

Most of the ground floor is given to Café Eighty-One, a red-upholstered restaurant by a Michelin-starred chef, with the colour drawn from the area's red-brick streets, while only two cars are on display.

Travertine, tactile textiles, brass and sculptural lighting deliberately mirror the car's interior, and a lower level holds private rooms for sales, meetings and customisation, including a navy Design Vault.
records.why: For Development sales galleries and Retail flagships, it shows how the discovery visit can lead with hospitality and place, holding the transaction back for a quieter private space once the visitor is engaged.
records.excerpt: Jaguar's spatial design lead framed the space not as a showroom but as a destination where architecture, culture, hospitality and craftsmanship meet.
records.oppText: Prospective buyers arrive at a chef-led café open to the public, with model homes nearby and a private lower-level room for finishes selection and contract conversations.

opps.title: Brand rooms that host
opps.text: Mall flagship units pair product display with a dwell-worthy food or lounge space so shoppers stay, meet friends and return without a purchase motive.

opps.title: Materials that tell the story
opps.text: Lobby and restaurant finishes echo a locally rooted palette so guests sense the setting and the brand from the threshold onward.

keyInsights: Giving most of the prime floor to hospitality rather than product turns a sales space into somewhere people choose to spend time.
Interiors that deliberately echo the product's own materials let visitors feel the brand before any sales conversation.
Separating a public, social ground floor from private rooms for purchase and customisation protects both the welcome and the decision.
Anchoring colour and material to the surrounding neighbourhood helps a brand space feel part of its place.

_bench.title: The Showroom That Serves Lunch First
_bench.short: Jaguar's Knightsbridge flagship gives most of its ground floor to a chef-led restaurant, showing two cars, with private sales rooms below.
_bench.lead: Visitors walk into Café Eighty-One, a welcoming red-toned restaurant open to anyone, with the Type 01 on display alongside. Those ready to go further move downstairs to private spaces, including a Design Vault, for sales and customisation discussions.

why.head: Hospitality lowers the threshold
why.body: A public restaurant invites people in who would never enter a car showroom to browse.

why.head: Space mirrors the product
why.body: Travertine, textiles and brass echo the car's interior so the brand is felt before it is explained.

why.head: Public above, private below
why.body: Separating social space from sales rooms keeps the welcome relaxed and the purchase conversation focused.

transfer.how: Flagship tenants could be encouraged to dedicate frontage to a café or lounge, with product consultations in quieter back-of-house rooms.
Hotel lobbies could use a locally inspired material palette and an open F&B space to draw in non-residents as a neighbourhood destination.
Community clubhouses could lead with a public café, with resident service and leasing conversations held in private rooms behind.

items.title: Cosm's Shared Reality cinematic experiences
items.dek: Cosm wraps classic films in 12K LED domes, themed venues and scene-timed menus, giving fans a reason to watch familiar titles together rather than at home.
summary: Cosm plays well-known films unchanged at the centre of 87-foot LED domes, while custom screen extensions carry each film's world around and above the audience as the story moves.
The experience reaches beyond the screen through lighting, sensory touches, interactive installations, and tasting and cocktail menus drawn from each film, served to the seat and timed to scenes.

Nearly all initial showings of the first title sold out within two weeks and the run was extended twice, and Universal has since joined Warner Bros. as a second studio partner, with a slate spanning sci-fi, family, horror and animation.
items.why: For Retail, it shows how a mall entertainment visit can become a destination worth leaving the sofa for, by building a shared, multi-sensory event around content people already love. For Hospitality, scene-timed themed menus point to F&B that is choreographed with the moment rather than simply served alongside it.
items.excerpt: Cosm leaves the original film untouched and instead enlarges the room around it, so the emotional pull of a familiar story grows when it is shared with a crowd.
items.oppText: Shoppers book a themed screening at the mall's cinema or event space where lighting, installations and a film-inspired menu turn a classic title into an evening out.

Extending a story into lighting, installations and food turns passive viewing into a full visit with more moments to remember.
Timing service to emotional beats makes F&B part of the narrative instead of an interruption.
Programming across genres, from family titles to horror, lets one venue reach very different audiences.

items.title: Climate of Change at OMSI
items.dek: Portland's science museum designed a climate exhibition around how visitors feel, not just what they learn, letting them choose their route by mood and readiness.
summary: The Oregon Museum of Science and Industry built its bilingual Climate of Change exhibition to address the anxiety and hopelessness people bring to the subject, structuring it as an emotional arc from heart to head to hope to hand.

Instead of a fixed route, the floor plan, shaped with advice from local Native American youth, opens onto four directions so visitors can pick a theatre of community stories, an immersive space, an art gallery or hands-on science according to whether they feel anxious, energised, curious or reflective.

Signature moments include a LIDAR-driven projection room where the environment grows from visitors who stand still, a quiet sphere space for reflection, and community-authored content that turns participation into co-ownership.
items.why: For Education, it shows how a school's learning spaces and open days can be designed around a student's or parent's emotional state as much as the content. For Community and Retail, it offers a model for public spaces that let visitors choose a calm or energetic path on each visit.
items.excerpt: OMSI designed the exhibition for the emotional experience of meeting climate change, on the view that feeling shapes a person's willingness to engage.
items.oppText: Students entering a school discovery space choose among a quiet reflection corner, a hands-on lab, a story wall of local voices or an art zone, each matched to how ready they feel to engage.

keyInsights: Designing for the emotion a visitor arrives with can matter as much as the information you want them to leave with.
Non-linear layouts that offer clear, named choices give people agency and let each visitor self-select the experience they are ready for.
Moving communities from consultation to co-ownership of content builds trust and lets people see themselves in a place.
Responsive technology can reward slowing down rather than activity, creating moments of presence and connection between strangers.

items.title: Jaguar designs Knightsbridge flagship to be a physical expression of the Type 01 electric car
items.dek: Jaguar has turned its London showroom into a destination led by a chef's restaurant, with interiors that echo its new car and private sales spaces below.
summary: Jaguar has rebuilt its Knightsbridge flagship as a destination rather than a conventional car showroom, and it is currently the only place where the public can see the new Type 01.

Most of the ground floor is given to Café Eighty-One, a red-upholstered restaurant by a Michelin-starred chef, with the colour drawn from the area's red-brick streets, while only two cars are on display.

Travertine, tactile textiles, brass and sculptural lighting deliberately mirror the car's interior, and a lower level holds private rooms for sales, meetings and customisation, including a navy Design Vault.
items.why: For Development sales galleries and Retail flagships, it shows how the discovery visit can lead with hospitality and place, holding the transaction back for a quieter private space once the visitor is engaged.
items.excerpt: Jaguar's spatial design lead framed the space not as a showroom but as a destination where architecture, culture, hospitality and craftsmanship meet.
items.oppText: Prospective buyers arrive at a chef-led café open to the public, with model homes nearby and a private lower-level room for finishes selection and contract conversations.

Interiors that deliberately echo the product's own materials let visitors feel the brand before any sales conversation.
Separating a public, social ground floor from private rooms for purchase and customisation protects both the welcome and the decision.
Anchoring colour and material to the surrounding neighbourhood helps a brand space feel part of its place.

items.title: Alaska Airlines Flagship Lounge by Graham Baba Architects
items.dek: At Seattle-Tacoma airport, Alaska Airlines moves away from the exclusive business lounge, using a staged entry and four distinct zones to offer every guest a refuge.
summary: Graham Baba Architects designed Alaska Airlines' flagship lounge at SeaTac as a warm, welcoming refuge from the concourse, deliberately moving away from the sleek, exclusive model of traditional airport lounges.

The space is divided into four lightly screened zones (an entry, a casual bistro, a quiet relaxation area and a bar), each with its own furniture, acoustics, materials and lighting so guests can choose the atmosphere that suits them.

A staged arrival sequence, from a wide concourse window and guiding oak frames to a fireplace view and a concierge desk, is combined with work by local fabricators and artists to root the experience in the Pacific Northwest.
items.why: For Hospitality and Retail, the lounge shows how an arrival sequence and a choice of distinct moods within one space can make a hotel lobby or a mall visitor lounge feel like a welcoming refuge, rather than a transactional waiting area.
items.excerpt: Alaska Airlines set out to replace the exclusive, business-like lounge with a warm home-away-from-home rooted in the Pacific Northwest, offering a range of spaces so every guest finds one where they feel at home.
items.oppText: Guests entering the hotel lobby move from a concierge welcome into lightly screened zones for coffee and conversation, quiet rest with lowered light and soft acoustics, and an evening bar, each with its own materials and seating.

Zoning a single space by atmosphere, with distinct acoustics, lighting and materials, lets guests self-select the experience they need.
A choreographed threshold, with a glimpse in, guiding elements, a focal view and a personal greeting, turns arrival into an invitation.
Commissioning local makers gives guests a tangible connection to place and differentiates a space from generic interiors.

items.title: Lark Hotels writes its own rules
items.dek: Lark Hotels runs more than 60 small properties across four brands, each designed around its own building, history and town rather than a single house aesthetic.
summary: Founded by a former educator turned innkeeper, Lark Hotels has grown to 63 properties across four brands, each built around the character of its building and destination rather than a uniform look.

Its creative director draws on a family background in innkeeping and antiques to fill historic homes with curated, one-of-a-kind pieces, while brands such as Blind Tiger add letters from local tastemakers describing how they would spend a day off in the city.
The portfolio ranges from opulent sea captains' mansions to landscape-led retreats and reinvented roadside motels, showing how a clear experiential philosophy can scale without becoming a commodity.
items.why: For Hospitality, Lark shows how the arrival and first evening can feel like being welcomed by a well-connected local friend rather than a chain. The same local-tastemaker idea could shape how Community teams welcome new residents in their first weeks in a neighbourhood.
items.excerpt: Lark's ambition is for a Blind Tiger stay to feel like being hosted by your best-connected friend, guided by locals who share how they would spend a day off.

Local voices, such as tastemakers sharing their day-off itinerary, make recommendations feel personal rather than generic concierge advice.
A portfolio can scale through several clearly differentiated brands that share one philosophy rather than one look.
Targeted design interventions, such as family-friendly rooms, can give ageing properties new relevance on limited budgets.

items.title: Light and shadow meet at One Bryant Park
items.dek: A new New York restaurant near Times Square uses Japanese ideas of filtered light and preserved shadow to turn three dining rooms into a calm retreat from the street.
summary: One Bryant Park on 42nd Street is a single restaurant offering three distinct dining experiences: a main dining room and bar, an omakase counter in Kumiko Room, and Kappo Sono, which is due to open in November.
Studio Canall designed each room with its own mood, tied together by the interplay of light and shadow and the meeting of Eastern and Western design.
Light is handled deliberately throughout, filtered through oak slats, backlit kumiko lattice and concealed fixtures, keeping darker pockets so that wood, plaster and metal textures can be felt.
items.why: For Hospitality and mall-based F&B in Retail, it shows how the moment a guest steps in from a busy street can be designed as a shift into calm, using lighting that keeps shadow rather than lighting a room evenly.
items.excerpt: The restaurant was conceived as a retreat from the Times Square bustle, meant to feel like standing in the shade of a forest.
items.oppText: Guests enter a hotel restaurant beneath a slatted timber canopy where light filters through and darker pockets are kept, so the room feels calmer and more intimate after dusk.

opps.title: Shade retreat threshold

keyInsights: Keeping deliberate pockets of shadow can make a space feel calmer and give natural materials more character than even, bright lighting.
A single venue can offer several distinct moods under one identity when a shared design idea ties the rooms together.
A façade that reads differently from the street and from inside can frame the arrival as a passage from city noise into retreat.
Cultural craft traditions, such as kumiko latticework, can be adapted to carry a sensory concept with authenticity.
